study: Lucas et al. perceived automation experiment
design: 2 x 2 experiment varying automation framing and actual control method
population: adult participants in a virtual-human health-screening interview
setting: semi-structured interview with the visually constant Ellie virtual human
intervention: told that the interviewer was fully computer-controlled
comparator: told that the interviewer was tele-operated by a human
measure: automated sadness detection and blind transcript ratings
author_claim: Computer framing increased behavioral indications of willingness to disclose.
evidence_statement: Participants in the computer-framed condition displayed more intense sadness and received higher blind-observer ratings of willingness to disclose in interview transcripts.
reviewer_interpretation: Converging behavioral and observer measures strengthen the mechanism result, but willingness and emotional display are not evidence that disclosures were accurate or clinically valid.
appraisal_framework: review-specific mixed-method risk-of-bias and applicability appraisal
applicability: Strong mechanism evidence about perceived automation; indirect evidence about autonomous interviewer performance.

study: Jacobsen et al. theory-based probe experiment
design: split-plot comparison of four probe types across three research stages
population: 64 U.S.-based English-speaking Prolific participants using desktop computers
setting: online HCI survey interviews about technology stress
intervention: descriptive, idiographic, clarifying, or explanatory LLM probes
comparator: other randomized probe groups across exploration, requirements, and evaluation tasks
measure: coded informativeness, relevance, specificity, and clarity
author_claim: Probe effectiveness depends on probe type and interview stage, with idiographic probes performing best overall.
evidence_statement: Across 1,287 responses, explanatory probes were less relevant, specific, and clear than several alternatives; idiographic probes outperformed explanatory probes on multiple outcomes in requirements and evaluation stages, while informativeness showed no overall probe difference.
reviewer_interpretation: Adaptive follow-up is not a unitary treatment: the purpose and research stage of a probe materially condition response quality.
appraisal_framework: review-specific mixed-method risk-of-bias and applicability appraisal
applicability: Strong design evidence for selecting probes; limited generalization beyond short online HCI survey tasks.

design: comparative user study across separately recruited system cohorts
population: adult volunteers recruited through Craigslist and flyers
setting: 15-25 minute semi-structured health interview with the Ellie virtual human
measure: post-interview listener item, System Usability Scale, and rapport measure
author_claim: Automation still lagged the Wizard-of-Oz system on important interaction-quality measures.
evidence_statement: The automatic system scored lower for being a good listener (3.56 vs 4.10, d=0.61), system usability (68.68 vs 74.37, d=0.44), and rapport (75.43 vs 80.71, d=0.44), with differences marked p<.05.
reviewer_interpretation: A system can sustain interviews while still losing meaningful conversational quality when human control is removed.
appraisal_framework: review-specific mixed-method risk-of-bias and applicability appraisal
overall_judgment: low confidence for causal effects; moderate confidence for feasibility
applicability: Directly relevant to embodied automated health interviewers and system-design tradeoffs.

study: Barari et al. four-module conversational survey experiment
design: three-arm randomized web-survey experiment with four embedded question modules
population: U.S. adults recruited from a proprietary non-probability panel and quota-sampled on age, gender, and education
setting: Inca web conversational survey, fielded July 15-17, 2024
intervention: LLM-generated confirmation probes or elaboration/relevance probes, with live zero-shot coding
measure: accuracy, precision, and recall against respondent confirmation and human coding
author_claim: Off-the-shelf live coding performed moderately well but produced inflated false positives.
evidence_statement: Respondent-confirmed accuracy ranged from 66.1% to 96.2% across tasks; agreement with independent human coding was lower for several tasks, and respondents selected 'none of the above' less often.
reviewer_interpretation: Live coding is task-dependent and respondent confirmation is not a neutral gold standard because the confirmation interaction itself can induce acquiescence.
appraisal_framework: review-specific mixed-method risk-of-bias and applicability appraisal
applicability: Directly applicable to LLM-assisted web survey interviewing; less direct for long-form qualitative or clinical interviews.

study: Barari et al. four-module conversational survey experiment
design: three-arm randomized web-survey experiment with four embedded question modules
population: U.S. adults recruited from a proprietary non-probability panel and quota-sampled on age, gender, and education
setting: Inca web conversational survey, fielded July 15-17, 2024
intervention: LLM-generated confirmation probes or elaboration/relevance probes, with live zero-shot coding
measure: attrition, interview duration, and normalized experience ratings
author_claim: AI probing imposed a small respondent-experience cost.
evidence_statement: Elaboration/relevance probing increased dropout by roughly 2-3 percentage points at the first question, doubled average completed-interview duration from about 3 to 6 minutes, and shifted ease, frustration, and satisfaction by less than 0.05 on normalized scales; confirmation probes had little effect.
reviewer_interpretation: Richer answers are not free: open-ended probing adds time and modest burden, while lightweight confirmation appears less costly.

study: Sun et al. child witness interview experiment
design: randomized comparison of LLM-formulated and naive-human-formulated interview questions
setting: online interview after viewing a witnessed mock-event video
intervention: real-time ChatGPT-3.5 question formulation, delivered by a human assistant
comparator: questions formulated and delivered by naive university-student interviewers
measure: blind-coded unique correct details, false details, and information per question
author_claim: LLM-formulated interviews elicited information more efficiently and with less false information than naive human interviewers.
evidence_statement: LLM interviews elicited similar unique correct details (8.50 vs 7.50, p=.290), more unique correct information per question (0.90 vs 0.46, p<.001), and less false information overall, while asking 471 questions versus 872 in the human condition.
reviewer_interpretation: This is unusually direct validity evidence, but it evaluates LLM-formulated questions read by a human and compares against naive—not trained forensic—interviewers.
appraisal_framework: review-specific mixed-method risk-of-bias and applicability appraisal
applicability: Strong evidence about question formulation and objective recall; indirect for autonomous adult qualitative interviewing.

study: Đuka and Njeguš conversational survey perception study
setting: 12-question rule-based Landbot survey distributed through WhatsApp
intervention: completion of a conversational survey chatbot
author_claim: Users in the Serbian sample remained unfamiliar with and distrustful of chatbots relative to human agents.
evidence_statement: Although 87% knew what a chatbot was, only 44% had used one; 88% preferred waiting for a human service agent, while 48% said they would use a brand lacking a human agent and 35% were unsure.
reviewer_interpretation: The study identifies a trust and familiarity barrier, but service-agent preference is not a direct test of research-interview preference and the descriptive sample offers no chatbot-versus-survey outcome comparison.
appraisal_framework: review-specific mixed-method risk-of-bias and applicability appraisal
applicability: Contextual trust and adoption evidence only; not an interviewer-effect estimate.

study: Lucas et al. perceived automation experiment
design: 2 x 2 experiment varying automation framing and actual control method
population: adult participants in a virtual-human health-screening interview
setting: semi-structured interview with the visually constant Ellie virtual human
intervention: told that the interviewer was fully computer-controlled
comparator: told that the interviewer was tele-operated by a human
measure: fear of self-disclosure and impression-management scales
author_claim: Believing a virtual interviewer was automated reduced barriers to disclosure.
evidence_statement: Compared with human-operation framing, computer framing produced lower self-reported fear of self-disclosure and impression management.
reviewer_interpretation: Perceived machine agency can reduce evaluation apprehension even when the visible agent is held constant; this isolates a psychological mechanism rather than overall interviewer quality.
appraisal_framework: review-specific mixed-method risk-of-bias and applicability appraisal
applicability: Strong mechanism evidence about perceived automation; indirect evidence about autonomous interviewer performance.

design: comparative user study across separately recruited system cohorts
population: adult volunteers recruited through Craigslist and flyers
setting: 15-25 minute semi-structured health interview with the Ellie virtual human
author_claim: The fully automatic system retained the prototype's ability to support personal sharing.
evidence_statement: Automatic and Wizard-of-Oz cohorts were similar on willingness to share (4.07 vs 4.03), comfort sharing (3.80 vs 3.92), and feeling good talking (3.60 vs 3.69); reported differences were small and not marked significant.
reviewer_interpretation: Feasibility is supported, but the nonrandomized cross-cohort comparison does not establish equivalence or causal effects on disclosure.
appraisal_framework: review-specific mixed-method risk-of-bias and applicability appraisal
overall_judgment: low confidence for causal effects; moderate confidence for feasibility
applicability: Directly relevant to embodied automated health interviewers and system-design tradeoffs.

study: Geiecke and Jaravel matched modality expert evaluation
design: multi-modality comparative evaluation with blinded transcript graders
population: behavioral-lab interview respondents across five qualitative topics
setting: 30-minute face-to-face, online text, or online voice interviews
intervention: GPT-4o AI interviewer using text or voice
comparator: trained human experts interviewing face-to-face or by online text chat
direction: AI voice comparable; AI text mixed
measure: sociology PhD ratings relative to hypothetical expert benchmarks
author_claim: Short AI-led interviews approached or exceeded trained-human interview quality under matched online constraints, especially with voice input.
evidence_statement: Against an online-text expert benchmark, mean grades were 3.93 for AI voice, 3.51 for human face-to-face, 2.98 for AI text, and 2.42 for human text; against a face-to-face benchmark they were 3.50, 3.53, 2.70, and 1.99 respectively, with 40 ratings per modality.
reviewer_interpretation: Blinded expert ratings support competitive transcript quality, but small modality cells, heterogeneous topics, and subjective benchmarks limit claims of equivalence.
appraisal_framework: review-specific mixed-method risk-of-bias and applicability appraisal
applicability: Direct comparison of AI and trained-human qualitative interview transcripts under online constraints.

study: Barari et al. four-module conversational survey experiment
design: three-arm randomized web-survey experiment with four embedded question modules
population: U.S. adults recruited from a proprietary non-probability panel and quota-sampled on age, gender, and education
setting: Inca web conversational survey, fielded July 15-17, 2024
intervention: LLM-generated confirmation probes or elaboration/relevance probes, with live zero-shot coding
measure: blind qualitative coding and textual information measures
author_claim: Elaboration and relevance probes improved some dimensions of response quality but not others.
evidence_statement: Probing increased specificity and explanation for the two opinion questions and increased word count and Shannon entropy, but did not improve completeness, relevance, lexical diversity, or KL divergence consistently.
reviewer_interpretation: The experiment supports a selective enrichment effect—more detail and explanation—not a general improvement in informational novelty or every quality dimension.

study: Geiecke and Jaravel meaning-in-life randomized comparison
design: randomized AI-led interview versus open-text survey comparison
population: U.S. adults recruited on Prolific with quotas for population representation
setting: online study about sources of meaning in life
comparator: three open-text survey questions covering the interview outline
outcome: clarity of thought about meaning in life
author_claim: AI-led interviewing improved respondents' clarity and produced richer material than open-text questions.
evidence_statement: In the randomized meaning-in-life study, 51.69% of AI-interview respondents said they could clearly pinpoint sources of meaning versus 41.18% in open text; 33.82% versus 41.57% said their thoughts were still evolving.
reviewer_interpretation: The comparison supports a reflective effect of the interview, although self-reported clarity is not an external validation of answer truth or qualitative depth.
appraisal_framework: review-specific mixed-method risk-of-bias and applicability appraisal
applicability: Direct for short online reflective interviews compared with open-text survey questions.
